name: rewrite a printed text under one hard constraint
one_line: A short printed text and the same content written out again under one limit: a counted number of words, or a reader who is nine.
how: The source goes on the same page and stays under twelve lines. Past that the sheet stops asking for a rewrite and starts measuring reading, and measuring it where whoever struggles will notice. Choose a badly written source — a notice in a hallway, a warranty, the manual of an appliance nobody owns — because rewriting something written well means making it worse, and whoever does it can feel that. Set one limit only. If it is a word count, print the count as separate short rules, fourteen of them, so nobody has to count. Then ask what was decided against: the line worth more than the rewrite.

knobs.effect: A hard word count makes the task about what to lose, which is where the difficulty sits; a named reader — somebody who is nine — makes it about register; asking for both at once produces neither.
Under twelve lines on the same page, anybody can begin; a chapter measures reading instead of rewriting, and a page of ten lines is already near the ceiling once the answer needs room too.

Printed as fourteen separate rules the limit is a visible fact and nobody counts; written as «about fourteen words» it is a rule to be kept, it gets kept loosely, and the difficulty goes out of the task.

knobs.knob: whether one buried word is pointed at
knobs.effect: Asking for the one word almost nobody knows to be ringed gives a finished piece of work to somebody who rewrites nothing, and that word is usually the reason the original exists.

where_the_work_is: In choosing the source. Badly written and short is better material than well written and short: there is something to be done to it, and no author on the other side to be measured against.
breaks: The source has to be printed beside the answer, so both compete for one A4 and twelve lines is about the ceiling. Short rules for a word count survive printing, but handwriting over a dashed rule scans back badly, so print them spaced and solid. On a display neither the source nor the answer fits.
